idiom_name: SortedMap<LocalDate, T> with floorEntry + default-argument accessor
implementation_notes: On the JVM the version in force is one call away: keep a SortedMap<LocalDate, T> (a TreeMap) and read floorEntry(when)?.value, with kotlinx-datetime's LocalDate as the Time Point (a Comparable date class with no time-zone ambiguity and explicit Clock/TimeZone for 'today'). Kotlin's default arguments replace the pattern's second accessor - fun salaryAt(when: LocalDate = today()) gives the no-argument form without a second method - and data-class values keep each stored version immutable. What replaces the classic structure: the sorted map's floor lookup plus the default parameter; the explicit temporal-collection class is still worth writing when validity can have gaps (floorEntry cannot express 'no value in force'), when two values may be valid at once, or when the history is persisted as its own table.
pitfalls: mutableMapOf() is a LinkedHashMap in insertion order, which behaves like an ordered store until versions arrive out of order - only a sorted/TreeMap-backed map gives the floor lookup.

java.time and kotlinx.datetime types are distinct classes with separate LocalDate/Instant definitions: mixing them in one model makes comparisons and conversions compile-error or, worse, silently reinterpret a value; pick one stack (kotlinx-datetime for multiplatform, java.time for JVM-only).

Default arguments are evaluated at the call site, so salaryAt() with no argument reads the ambient clock - inject the Clock/TimeZone (as above) so tests and replays are reproducible and so 'today' is a business-zone date.

sortedMapOf/TreeMap is not thread-safe and put at an existing key overwrites the version: a same-day correction leaves no trace unless the key carries a revision, and concurrent updates need explicit confinement or locking.
